description: Conjugal roles, the domestic division of labour and how family relationships changed in modern Britain.
content_html:
What Are Conjugal Roles?

Conjugal roles refer to the roles performed by each partner within a couple relationship. Sociologists distinguish between two broad patterns. Joint conjugal roles describe partnerships where tasks, decision making and leisure are shared between partners. Segregated conjugal roles describe partnerships where male and female partners have clearly defined separate tasks — typically, the man in paid employment and the woman in domestic work and child rearing. Understanding how these patterns have changed — and whether they have genuinely become more equal — is at the heart of the families and relationships topic.

The Domestic Division of Labour

The domestic division of labour refers to how unpaid household tasks and child rearing are distributed within the home. Sociologists study a wide range of activities: cooking, cleaning, laundry, child care, disciplining children, managing household finances, arranging leisure activities and making major household decisions. The central question is whether this division is equal between partners, and whether it has become more equal as women have entered the paid workforce in greater numbers.

Functionalist View: Parsons and Complementary Roles

Talcott Parsons argued that the gender-divided conjugal role pattern — the man performing the instrumental role (breadwinner, financial provider) and the woman performing the expressive role (homemaker, emotional carer) — was both functionally efficient and naturally grounded. From this perspective, segregated conjugal roles are complementary: each partner contributes different but equally important tasks. Parsons presented this division as meeting the needs of modern industrial society, where paid employment demands geographical mobility and one adult must maintain the home while the other moves with work.

Peter Willmott and Michael Young (1973) argued that conjugal roles were becoming more equal over time. Their research suggested the modern family was becoming “symmetrical” — meaning that partners were increasingly sharing domestic tasks and leisure. Willmott and Young described the symmetrical family as one where roles are not identical but broadly equal in the time and effort each partner contributes. They linked this change to the principle of stratified diffusion: lifestyle changes begin among middle-class families and gradually spread to working-class families. For Willmott and Young, the trend towards symmetry represented a positive “march of progress” in family life.

Oakley’s Feminist Critique: The Myth of the Symmetrical Family

Ann Oakley directly challenged Willmott and Young’s optimistic picture. Her research on housework, published in The Sociology of Housework (1974), found that the domestic division of labour remained profoundly unequal despite changes in women’s employment. Oakley argued that the conventional family — with its gender-divided roles — was not disappearing but persisting in new forms. She criticised Willmott and Young’s methodology, noting that their threshold for male domestic participation was very low: men who helped with housework at least once a week were counted as “participating”.

Oakley developed the concept of the double shift to describe the burden on women who work in paid employment but continue to perform the majority of domestic labour at home. Rather than replacing domestic work, women’s entry into the paid labour market added a second shift to their day. Some feminist sociologists have further extended this to the concept of the triple shift — paid work, domestic labour and the emotional management of family relationships — capturing the full range of labour that women typically carry out.

Key Fact

Willmott and Young (1973) argued that conjugal roles were becoming more equal through the “symmetrical family” and the principle of stratified diffusion. Oakley challenged this as a myth — her research showed the domestic division of labour remained unequal and that women performed a “double shift” of paid work plus domestic labour.

Contemporary Issues: Dual Career Families, Decision Making and Leisure

Dual career families — where both partners are in paid employment — have grown significantly. This raises questions about how domestic labour is redistributed when both partners work. Research consistently shows that even in dual career households, women perform more domestic tasks and child care than their male partners on average. Decision making — who has the final say on major financial or household decisions — continues to be gendered in many households, with men retaining greater influence over major financial decisions. Money management patterns vary: in some families one partner controls all finances; in others both have independent access to income. Leisure activities also differ: research suggests men have more free leisure time than women in couples, where women’s leisure is more frequently interrupted by domestic and caring responsibilities.

Child-Centred Families, Boomerang Children and the Sandwich Generation

The specification identifies three further concepts about how family relationships have changed:

  • Child-centred families: post-war British families became increasingly organised around the needs and wellbeing of children. Children’s emotional development, education and leisure became central concerns of parenting. This represents a significant shift from earlier generations in which children were expected to contribute economically to the household from a young age.
  • Boomerang children: adult children who return to the parental home after living independently, typically due to high housing costs, unemployment or relationship breakdown. High property prices in many parts of the UK have made this trend particularly pronounced, with many people in their twenties and thirties unable to afford to live independently.
  • Sandwich generation: people in middle age who face the dual responsibility of caring for both their own (sometimes adult) children and their ageing parents at the same time. The combination of extended life expectancy and delayed childbearing has made this “squeezed middle” experience more common. The caring burden falls disproportionately on women.
Key Fact

The boomerang generation (adult children returning home due to housing costs) and the sandwich generation (middle-aged adults caring for both children and parents simultaneously) are two contemporary features of British family life that reflect both economic pressures and demographic change. Both tend to increase the caring burden on women.

The “New Man” — the idea of a modern father who shares fully in domestic tasks and child rearing — is frequently cited in media and everyday discussion as evidence that conjugal roles have become equal. Feminist sociologists challenge this. Oakley argued that media representations of involved fatherhood are not backed by empirical data: the domestic division of labour remains unequal across most households. More men take paternity leave than in previous generations, but research suggests the distribution of daily, routine domestic tasks (cooking, cleaning, laundry, managing children’s schedules) continues to fall disproportionately on women. The “New Man” may be a cultural ideal rather than a sociological reality.
exam_tip_html:
On a 2-mark Define question for “double shift”, make sure you include both components: paid employment AND unpaid domestic labour. Mentioning only one component earns just 1 mark. A full answer: “The double shift refers to the situation in which women in paid employment also continue to perform the majority of unpaid domestic labour at home, effectively working two shifts in a day.”

On a 12-mark Evaluate about conjugal roles, the highest marks are earned by presenting the Willmott and Young symmetrical family argument AND Oakley’s feminist counter, then adding a third perspective (Parsons’ functionalist complementary roles argument or the Marxist feminist view that domestic labour benefits capitalism). Students who describe the debate but reach no supported conclusion stay in the Secure band. A Mastering answer explicitly weighs the evidence: is there more support for Willmott and Young’s “march of progress” or for Oakley’s “myth”? Use contemporary evidence (dual career families, sandwich generation) to support your judgement.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Conjugal roles describe how partners divide paid work, domestic tasks and child rearing. Joint conjugal roles are relatively equal; segregated conjugal roles assign distinct tasks by gender. The domestic division of labour includes decision making, money management, child rearing, household tasks and leisure.
  • Willmott and Young (1973) argued the family was becoming symmetrical through the principle of stratified diffusion. Oakley challenged this as a myth — her research showed the domestic division of labour remained unequal and that women performed a double shift (and sometimes a triple shift) of paid work, domestic labour and emotional management.
  • Contemporary trends include child-centred families, boomerang children (returning home due to housing costs) and the sandwich generation (caring for both children and ageing parents). These trends tend to place additional caring burdens on women, supporting Oakley’s argument that gender inequality in the home persists.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes 'segregated conjugal roles'?
A) Both partners share domestic tasks and leisure activities equally
B) Male and female partners have distinct, separate tasks — typically the man in paid work and the woman in domestic labour
C) One partner earns while the other manages the family finances
D) Roles are negotiated week by week depending on work schedules
practice_questions.marks: B) Male and female partners have distinct, separate tasks — typically the man in paid work and the woman in domestic labour [1 mark]

1 mark for identifying that it refers to women in paid employment; 1 mark for explaining that they also continue to perform the majority of unpaid domestic labour at home. Example: 'The double shift refers to the situation in which women who are in paid employment also continue to perform the majority of unpaid domestic labour at home, effectively working two shifts in a day.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe the concept of the 'sandwich generation'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the sandwich generation as middle-aged people responsible for caring for both their children and ageing parents simultaneously. 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'The combination of extended life expectancy (older parents living longer and needing care) and delayed childbearing (people having children later in life) means that many middle-aged adults find themselves simultaneously responsible for caring for dependent children and for their own elderly parents. This creates significant time and financial pressure, and the caring burden tends to fall disproportionately on women.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the functionalist view of conjugal roles within the family.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for naming Parsons and the functionalist perspective. 1 mark for describing the instrumental role (male breadwinner, financial provider). 1 mark for describing the expressive role (female homemaker and emotional carer). 1 mark for an explanation of why Parsons saw this as functional: the roles are complementary, not unequal — each is different but equally important, and together they meet the family's needs in a geographically mobile industrial economy.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that conjugal role relationships have become more equal in contemporary British families.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or more contrasting perspectives developed with named sociologists, sociological vocabulary used accurately, a supported judgement. For growing equality: Willmott and Young's symmetrical family thesis (1973) — joint conjugal roles increasingly common through the principle of stratified diffusion; growth of dual career families; more men taking paternity leave. Against: Oakley's feminist critique — the domestic division of labour remains unequal; women perform the double shift or triple shift; decision making and money management favour men; the sandwich generation burden falls disproportionately on women. Parsons as context (functionalist endorsement of gender-divided roles). Supported conclusion.

Secure: Both sides present, at least one named sociologist, judgement at the end.

Developing: Relevant points, one-sided or undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic description, few or no named sociologists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that the domestic division of labour remains fundamentally unequal between men and women in British families.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against, at least two named sociologists or perspectives developed in detail, sociological vocabulary used accurately, a clear supported judgement that weighs the evidence. For ongoing inequality: Oakley's research on housework (1974) — domestic division of labour unequal despite women's employment; the double and triple shift; research showing women in dual career households still perform more domestic tasks; the sandwich generation burden falling on women; decision making research showing men retain greater financial authority. Against (some movement towards equality): Willmott and Young (1973) — the symmetrical family and stratified diffusion suggest change is real; growth of dual career families; legal changes promoting gender equality. Parsons's functionalist argument as a descriptive starting point but challenged. Sociological vocabulary (segregated conjugal roles, symmetrical family, double shift, principle of stratified diffusion, patriarchy, conventional family) used accurately. Comparison and contrast of perspectives explicit. Substantiated conclusion that weighs the evidence.

Secure: Most relevant arguments present, both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement present.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic points, mainly description, few or no named sociologists, little judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which sociologists argued in 1973 that the family was becoming 'symmetrical' with roles more equally shared between partners?
Oakley used the term 'double shift' to describe women who perform paid employment AND also continue to perform most of the _____ at home.
Conjugal roles in which both partners share tasks, decision making and leisure relatively equally are called _____ conjugal roles.
Willmott and Young's argument that lifestyle changes begin among the middle class and gradually spread to the working class is called the principle of _____ diffusion.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: Adult children who return to the parental home, often due to housing costs or unemployment
Middle-aged people caring for both their own children and their ageing parents simultaneously
The combined burden of paid work, domestic labour and emotional management of family relationships

A pattern in which partners share domestic tasks, paid work and decision making relatively equally.
A pattern in which male and female partners have distinct separate tasks — typically the man in paid work, the woman in domestic labour.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the domestic division of labour?
flashcard_questions.a: The distribution of unpaid household tasks and child rearing responsibilities between partners within the home.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the double shift, according to Oakley?
flashcard_questions.a: The situation in which women in paid employment also perform the majority of unpaid domestic labour at home.
The combined burden of paid work, domestic labour and emotional management of family relationships, typically borne by women.

flashcard_questions.q: How did Oakley criticise Willmott and Young's research on the symmetrical family?
flashcard_questions.a: She argued their threshold for male participation was set too low — helping with housework once a week counted as participating.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the principle of stratified diffusion?
flashcard_questions.a: Willmott and Young's argument that lifestyle changes begin among the middle class and gradually spread to the working class.
Adult children who return to the parental home, typically due to high housing costs, unemployment or relationship breakdown.
People in middle age who are simultaneously responsible for caring for their own children and their ageing parents.
The female nurturing role focused on the emotional wellbeing of children and management of the home.

glossary_terms.definition: The roles and responsibilities performed by partners within a marriage or cohabiting relationship, including paid work, domestic labour and child rearing.
The distribution of unpaid household tasks and child rearing responsibilities between partners within the home.
The phenomenon in which women who work in paid employment also continue to perform the majority of unpaid domestic labour at home.
Willmott and Young's term for a family in which partners share domestic tasks and leisure relatively equally, though not necessarily identically.
Oakley's term for the arrangement in which the woman is the primary homemaker and the man the primary breadwinner, characterised by segregated conjugal roles.
Adult children who return to the parental home after living independently, often due to high housing costs, unemployment or relationship breakdown.
People in middle age who face the dual responsibility of caring for both their own children and their ageing parents simultaneously.
Willmott and Young's argument that lifestyle changes begin among the middle class and gradually spread down to the working class.
